summary.topic: How safe and available drinking water is in our community, compared with the global picture reported by the World Health Organization (WHO).
key_points: WHO reports that in 2022 at least 1.7 billion people used a drinking-water source contaminated with faeces.
Contaminated water can spread diarrhoea, cholera, dysentery, typhoid and polio.
This report compares those global facts with a small survey of water sources in our area (your data).
summary.takeaway: Safe water depends on protecting sources from contamination; your findings will show how our community compares.

blocks.title: How to use this draft
blocks.text: The structure, background and references are ready. Every green **YOUR TURN** box marks work that must be yours: your survey, your results and your own analysis. Delete these boxes when you have written those parts.

Safe water is needed for drinking, cooking and hygiene. In 2010 the UN General Assembly explicitly recognised the human right to water and sanitation (WHO, 2023). This report looks at where households in our area get their drinking water and how safe those sources are.
**Aim:** to find out which water sources households in our area use and whether they are protected from contamination.
ADD YOUR research question in one sentence, and name the area you studied (village, ward or suburb).
The WHO fact sheet on drinking-water gives the global picture:

blocks.text: WHO defines a *safely managed* service as one located on premises, available when needed and free from contamination. It states that microbial contamination from faeces poses the greatest risk to drinking-water safety.

ADD YOUR local background: what water sources are common in your area (boreholes, wells, rivers, piped water)? Use a source you can name, such as your local council or an interview with a community health worker.
A simple survey method that suits a school project:

items: Choose a sample of households (for example 20) and ask permission before each interview.
Ask: main drinking-water source, distance to it, whether it is covered or protected, and whether water is treated (boiled, chlorinated) at home.
Observe each source if it is safe to do so: is it covered, fenced, near a toilet or animals?
Record answers in a table (see Table 2).

items: How does the share of households using protected sources compare with the global figure in Table 1?
Which sources might be at risk of contamination from faeces, and why?
What could households, the school or the council do to make water safer?
